title: Federal Trade Commission v. QT, Inc.
lead: Sellers market a metal bracelet with dramatic pain-relief testimonials, scientific claims, and a thirty-day guarantee. After a bench trial, the court examines the evidence behind those representations and distinguishes the responsible manager from an officer who lacked control or knowledge.

actors.name: Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
actors.role: Public enforcement plaintiff challenging bracelet advertising and refunds.

actors.name: QT, Q-Ray Company, and Bio-Metal
actors.role: Corporate sellers of the Spanish-made metal bracelet.

actors.name: Que Te Park, also called Andrew Park
actors.role: President of all three companies and controller of QT and Q-Ray Company.

actors.name: Jung Joo Park
actors.role: Corporate secretary and Park’s wife, separately evaluated for individual liability.

actors.name: Magistrate Judge Denlow
actors.role: Consenting trial judge issuing findings and remedial directions.

proceedings: The FTC sued in 2003 and obtained asset-freeze and stipulated preliminary relief.
After a seven-day consent bench trial, the court found the corporations and Que Te Park liable on all counts but found for Jung Joo Park.
The memorandum ordered overlapping monetary relief and directed an anti-deception injunction, with final judgment to be submitted and entered later.
limits: This transforms the canonical 2006 trial-opinion brief without a fresh audit or claim of current § 13(b) remedial authority. The narrative reports Rule 52 findings, not allegations assumed true. The newer 2005 infomercial was outside trial. Later final-judgment entry or form is not inferred from scheduled directions, and disgorgement is not added cumulatively to all refunds.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The bracelet becomes a direct-consumer health product
paragraphs: Que Te Park, also known as Andrew Park, encountered a C-shaped Spanish-made metal bracelet in 1994 and began American sales in 1996. He was president of QT, Q-Ray Company, and Bio-Metal and controlled the first two. Wholesale costs ranged from $7.50 to $28; retail prices were $49.95 to $249.95.

Direct-consumer infomercials began in 2000. Four lengthy versions, websites, brochures, and packaging promised immediate, significant, or complete relief from many forms of pain. Testimonials described vanished back and joint pain; hosts reinforced them with purported scientific mechanisms and demonstrations. Advertising also promised an unconditional thirty-day refund.

sections.title: Available studies fail to support the promoted benefit
sections.cue: What did the sellers know about their substantiation?
paragraphs: Graduate student DeAnn Trapp’s first report contained pain and placebo results that did not substantiate the advertised benefit. At the company’s request, the version given to QT omitted that material, which remained in her thesis. Her second study was also methodologically inadequate.

Other reports suffered from weak blinding, unexplained populations and measurements, missing raw data, inadequate comparison groups, and uncertain product identity. Foreign studies sometimes addressed a supposedly magnetic Bio-Ray bracelet without showing equivalence to nonmagnetic Q-Ray. A two-paragraph Japanese letter supplied no pain-relief evidence.

The Mayo study found improvement in active and placebo groups without a statistically significant difference. Criticizing its methodology could not turn it into affirmative support. QT continued the challenged infomercial after learning the result. Park also offered inconsistent ionization explanations without substantiating manufacturing or a maintained physiologically meaningful charge.

sections.title: The FTC brings enforcement and the court conducts a full trial
sections.cue: How did the judge evaluate the advertising message?
paragraphs: The Federal Trade Commission sued May 27, 2003. An asset-freeze temporary restraining order followed May 29 and a stipulated preliminary injunction June 11. By consent, Magistrate Judge Denlow conducted a seven-day bench trial between June 6 and July 11, 2006, then made Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 52 findings.

The court assessed each advertisement’s overall impression from testimonials, onscreen words, hosts, and qualifications. Brief, inconspicuous warnings of varying results or uncertain scientific consensus did not undo prominent efficacy and proof claims. Their express or obvious implied character permitted direct evaluation without a consumer survey or psychology expert, although an expert offered for consumer-perception testimony would still need proper qualifications.

Deception required a material representation, omission, or practice likely to mislead reasonable consumers. Express and important health claims were presumptively material under the applied precedents. Pain relief and proof drove purchase, and the guarantee reduced perceived risk.

The bracelet was a statutory device because its advertised intended use mitigated pain and affected bodily function, regardless of actual success. No principal chemical or metabolic operation was shown; the court also explained the alternative drug classification if such action were established. Denying effectiveness did not remove the promoted product from false-advertising law.

sections.title: The medical claims fail both reasonable-basis and claimed-proof scrutiny
sections.cue: Why did placebo response not establish inherent efficacy?
paragraphs: For Count I, defendants had to identify substantiation they claimed, while the FTC retained the burden to prove inadequacy. A simple efficacy claim differed from an establishment claim asserting a particular proof level. The former required an assessment of product, claim, error costs, truthful benefits, substantiation cost, and accepted expert standards; the latter required the represented proof.

Six experts testified. For these strong health claims, competent and reliable evidence required a well-conducted randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. This requirement concerned medical advertising, not sale of jewelry for appearance or enjoyment. Even defendants’ statistician acknowledged serious deficiencies in several studies. Anecdotes could not fill those gaps, and Mayo remained the strongest available study without proving the claim.

The court preferred the FTC physicist’s analysis to speculation about implanted ions. A traditional-Chinese-medicine witness neither placed ionization within that tradition nor supplied a scientific basis for this bracelet; a placebo expert offered no product-specific efficacy proof.

Pantron and Acu-Dot, precedents addressing placebo-based defenses, supported rejecting subjective improvement as proof of represented inherent effectiveness. The court’s discussion assumed placebo-only benefit for that analysis rather than making a universal clinical finding about every possible mechanism. Count I violated Federal Trade Commission Act §§ 5 and 12. Count II independently succeeded because claims that tests proved relief were unsupported by the studies, making falsity and inadequate basis converge.

sections.title: The refund promise and individual responsibility require separate findings
sections.cue: Why did one officer avoid liability?
paragraphs: Many online buyers and buyers of some styles received a shorter refund window despite the prominent thirty-day promise. A less visible website link disclosed the shorter period, but infomercials sent viewers there without warning. Later uniform thirty-day treatment applied only prospectively, leaving earlier ten-day-policy denials uncorrected. That proved Count III. Ordinary processing delays during rapid growth were not a separate violation.

A prior Illinois consumer-class-action directed verdict for Park did not preclude federal enforcement. The FTC was neither party nor privy to private claimants; it vindicated a public statutory interest. Fairness also opposed preclusion, and identical issues were not shown because private consumer reliance differed from federal individual-liability requirements.

Individual responsibility required participation or authority to control plus requisite knowledge, not subjective intent to defraud. Park approved advertising and controlled research and policies with knowledge. Jung Joo Park’s secretary title and bank-signature authority did not establish participation, control, or knowledge. Her office, shipping, and employee-help functions and marriage to Park did not fill those gaps.

sections.title: The court orders overlapping financial relief and an anti-deception injunction
sections.cue: What did the September memorandum actually require?
paragraphs: Applying § 13(b) equitable precedents then governing, the court rejected an absolute net-profit ceiling and distinguished direct consumer losses from payments retained by nonparty intermediaries. It ordered $22.5 million profits disgorgement plus interest and full-refund eligibility for January 1, 2000–June 30, 2003 buyers, capped at $87,019,840 in net direct-consumer sales.

The remedies overlapped: $10 million in refunds would leave a $22.5 million total obligation, $40 million refunded would produce a $40 million total, and $95 million claimed would be capped at $87,019,840. The opinion did not add another $22.5 million to every refund total.

On September 8, 2006, the court directed judgment jointly and severally against the three corporations and Que Te Park on all counts and for Jung Joo Park on all counts. Permanent relief was to prevent deceptive conduct involving this bracelet or similar products, not categorically prohibit every future bracelet sale. Claims about a November 2005 infomercial remained outside this trial.

The parties were to submit a proposed final judgment by September 22, with later entry scheduled for September 28. Those directions do not establish the form actually entered later. No separate writing accompanied the trial opinion.
